title: The Impact of AI on Paralegals — NALP (UK) educational think piece by Robin Ghurbhurun
pub: Artificial Lawyer (educational think piece by NALP — the UK National Association of Licensed Paralegals — for Artificial Lawyer)
author: Robin Ghurbhurun

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s copilot framing and its central claim that human verification remains necessary because legal AI can fabricate details. It also endorses efficiency and accuracy benefits for selected tasks, but offers illustrative claims rather than measured evidence and does not assess whether verification costs offset those gains.
qs: In most systems already in use which employ AI, the technology acts to support and improve the work of humans.
A human (paralegal) interface with AI will be essential for the foreseeable future particularly in areas such as identifying AI 'hallucination' of detail in responses and verifying outputs generated.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Ghurbhurun aligns closely with the cluster’s principal proposition: AI will automate and reshape bounded legal tasks rather than eliminate human legal roles, while paralegals move toward higher-value work, quality control and verification. He also supports the cluster’s emphasis on hallucination risk, user capability and continued human oversight, though he does not substantially address apprenticeship risks or organisational evaluation.
qs: In most systems already in use which employ AI, the technology acts to support and improve the work of humans.
A human (paralegal) interface with AI will be essential for the foreseeable future particularly in areas such as identifying AI 'hallucination' of detail in responses and verifying outputs generated.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Ghurbhurun supports the cluster’s central proposition by portraying AI as substituting for administrative and information-processing tasks while complementing paralegals in advice, quality control and verification. He anticipates changed role content rather than wholesale replacement, but offers predictions rather than evidence of staffing or employment outcomes.
qs: For paralegals, the deployment of AI tools, is likely to lead to work involving more nuanced business-led advice rather than collation and administration of data.
A human (paralegal) interface with AI will be essential for the foreseeable future particularly in areas such as identifying AI 'hallucination' of detail in responses and verifying outputs generated.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Ghurbhurun directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI will automate selected information-heavy tasks while redesigning, rather than eliminating, human legal work. He anticipates continued paralegal involvement and a shift toward advice, quality control and contractual safeguarding, while recognising risks from inaccurate AI interactions.
qs: For example, he writes: 'A human (paralegal) interface with AI will be essential for the foreseeable future.' Read on.*  AI is clearly transforming how we approach, execute, and innovate in our work, and paralegals are as impacted by this as any group of professionals.
For paralegals, the deployment of AI tools, is likely to lead to work involving more nuanced business-led advice rather than collation and administration of data.

kp.k: Automation could shift paralegals toward advisory and quality-control work
kp.d: Ghurbhurun asserts that AI has capacity to automate up to 40% of the average workday, without identifying a supporting study or a paralegal-specific measurement. He predicts that paralegals' work will move from data collation and administration toward nuanced business-led advice, quality control, and optimising and safeguarding contractual arrangements.
qs: With the capacity to automate up to 40% of the average workday, the implications for efficiency and productivity are profound, especially in sectors reliant on the processing and analysis of vast information volumes, such as the legal field.
For paralegals, the deployment of AI tools, is likely to lead to work involving more nuanced business-led advice rather than collation and administration of data.
In addition, there will be a focus on quality control and the optimisation and safeguarding of contractual arrangements.

kp.k: Legal prompt engineering offers a potential paralegal specialism
kp.d: The author identifies an opportunity for paralegals to become expert legal prompt writers supporting AI training and deployment. He argues that prompt quality affects legal accuracy, illustrating how contract-analysis prompts could identify clauses and contextual implications, and claims benefits for contract review, due diligence and research. These are proposed capabilities and benefits rather than measured results. Developing this specialism requires both legal knowledge and understanding of how AI processes language.
qs: There's also potential for paralegals to up-skill and become expert legal 'prompt writers' (who are used for effective training and deployment of legal AI).
Understandably and critically, in law the stakes are high: a poorly constructed prompt could lead to misinterpretation or legal inaccuracy.
This capability transforms tasks such as contract review, due diligence and even legal research, saving countless hours while improving accuracy.
Mastering the field requires not only familiarity with legal terminology and concepts, but also an understanding of how AI models process and respond to language.

kp.k: AI is framed as augmentation rather than human replacement
kp.d: Ghurbhurun argues that most AI systems already in use support human work, and reports signs that familiarity improves effective use and reduces replacement concerns. He also reports that most surveyed workers perceive improved performance and working conditions, but supplies no survey identification, sample size, dates or evidence that respondents were specifically legal workers.
qs: In most systems already in use which employ AI, the technology acts to support and improve the work of humans.
Most surveyed workers say that AI has improved both their performance and their working conditions.

kp.k: Human verification remains essential because AI can fabricate details
kp.d: The author predicts a continuing need for a human paralegal interface, particularly to identify hallucinated details and check generated outputs. He illustrates the risk with ChatGPT falsely accusing an American law professor of sexual harassment while citing a nonexistent Washington Post report. He explains that predictive language generation can produce factual errors whose human-seeming presentation persuades users, and asserts that output quality depends on input quality.
qs: A human (paralegal) interface with AI will be essential for the foreseeable future particularly in areas such as identifying AI 'hallucination' of detail in responses and verifying outputs generated.
In one example ChatGPT falsely accused an American law professor of sexual harassment and cited a non-existent Washington Post report in the process.
This means factual errors are possible, but the human-seeming response can sometimes convince users that the answer is correct.

It's worth noting that currently even generative AI can only produce 'new' content by recycling what it has already been trained on: 'Garbage In Garbage Out' – the quality of output is determined by the quality of the input.

kp.k: Paralegals could address fraud and AI liability questions
kp.d: Ghurbhurun proposes client-identity checks, detection of fraudulent transactions and AI-voiced phishing scams, and assistance identifying liability between AI providers and deployers as potential paralegal responsibilities. He asserts that paralegals can make distinctions AI cannot make itself; the document offers no case evidence or legal analysis establishing that division of responsibility.
qs: Paralegals could verify the identity of clients, catch fraudulent transactions and AI voiced phishing scams, and help identify where legal liability lies in the AI value chain; providers (creators) or deployers (users).
AI cannot make these distinctions itself, paralegals can.

kp.k: Practical workflow expertise could position paralegals as adoption leaders
kp.d: The author recommends prioritising targeted applications over novelty and learning how automation benefits law firms or in-house teams. He argues that paralegals' insight into day-to-day practice processes positions them to lead adoption by identifying beneficial applications while understanding technological limitations and pitfalls. This is a recommendation and prospective role, not a documented organisational outcome.
qs: I believe, paralegals should focus on targeted applications of AI rather than novelty factors.
It's worth remembering that, very often, it is the paralegals who have the best insight into the day-to-day processes required to keep a practice running effectively.

This means that they can act as a vanguard of AI experts who understand where AI adoption will bring the most benefit, at the same time as having an understanding of the limitations and also the pit falls of the technology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Robin Ghurbhurun predicts that AI will automate routine work and shift paralegals toward advice, quality control, contractual safeguards and legal prompt engineering rather than simply replace them.
pts.d: Ghurbhurun states that AI has the capacity to automate up to 40% of the average workday, presenting this as a general productivity potential with particular relevance to information-intensive legal work, not as a measured paralegal-specific displacement rate. He expects paralegal work to move away from data collation and administration toward nuanced business-led advice, quality control and optimising and safeguarding contracts. He identifies legal prompt writing as an upskilling opportunity and characterises prompt engineering as a fundamental change in legal professionals' interaction with technology. His illustrative contract-analysis example claims that well-designed prompts can enable identification of clauses and their contextual implications, saving time and improving accuracy in contract review, due diligence and legal research.

pts.k: Ghurbhurun presents AI primarily as human augmentation, with an enduring paralegal role in verifying outputs and addressing AI-related risks.
pts.d: He claims that most systems already in use support and improve human work and that growing familiarity helps firms use AI effectively while reducing replacement concerns. He predicts an essential human paralegal interface for checking fabricated details and verifying AI outputs. He also proposes roles in client identity verification, detecting fraudulent transactions and AI-voiced phishing, and identifying whether liability rests with AI providers or deployers. He explicitly asserts that AI cannot itself make these distinctions. Finally, he argues that paralegals' understanding of everyday practice processes positions them to lead targeted AI adoption in firms and in-house teams. These are predictions and proposed roles, not reported evidence of realised changes in paralegal employment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on professional commentary, an unattributed automation estimate and worker-survey assertion, an illustrative task example, and a reported instance of fabricated AI output.
pts.d: Ghurbhurun writes as a NALP governing-board member and Jisc managing director for Further Education and Skills. The document supplies no citation, method, population or measurement period for the 'up to 40%' automation estimate, and no named survey, sample or figures for its statement that most surveyed workers report better performance and conditions. The contract-analysis discussion is illustrative rather than a documented deployment or benchmark. To support the need for verification, he recounts ChatGPT falsely accusing an American law professor of sexual harassment and citing a nonexistent Washington Post report; the document does not identify the professor or provide a citation. This is a reported fabrication incident, not a court-sanctions case or measured hallucination rate. Claims about role transformation, AI-transition leadership and AI's inability to make the stated risk and liability distinctions are offered as authorial argument, without supporting employment data or comparative tests.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2025 piece combines claims about current augmentation with undated future role changes and a human-verification requirement lasting for the 'foreseeable future'.
pts.d: No adoption deadline or quantified employment trajectory is given. The shift in paralegal tasks is described as 'likely', prompt-writing careers as having 'potential', and risk-management tasks as things paralegals 'could' do. Benefits depend on targeted applications, familiarity with the technology, well-designed prompts, input quality and combined legal and AI expertise. Ghurbhurun warns that poorly constructed prompts can produce misinterpretation or legal inaccuracy and that fluent responses can persuade users to accept factual errors. He qualifies his account of generative AI's dependence on training material as applying 'currently'. His preparation advice is to build understanding now to participate in future adoption, rather than pursue novelty.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Paralegals are the central affected group, with implications for law firms, in-house legal teams, clients and AI providers and deployers.
pts.d: In this UK NALP educational piece, paralegals are presented as moving from routine information administration into advice, contractual quality control, prompt engineering, human verification and AI-adoption leadership. Firms and corporate in-house teams are potential beneficiaries of better-targeted automation, efficiency and accuracy; no firm size or market tier is specified. Clients are implicated through identity checks and fraud protection, while people described in AI outputs face risks from fabricated allegations. AI creators and users are implicated as potential bearers of liability that paralegals could help identify. The article does not forecast paralegal headcount, pay, billing-model changes or access-to-justice outcomes.
